<reason>CON built a genuinely sharp attack: the timing contradiction (aggregate-later mechanisms vs. the courier hurt Thursday), the compliance-moat concern, and an alternative of decoupling benefits from work status. The Pressure Questions round produced real clash — B's Q2 exposed a live tension in A's own rationing story (if no platform can see the total, how does hour-capping work?), forcing A to retreat from a vivid "Uber caps her hours" claim to a softer "probabilistic hedging" claim. That retreat is a real concession. Meanwhile PRO successfully neutralized A's core mechanism objections by analogizing to real, familiar multi-payer systems (unemployment insurance summing multiple employers, existing 1099 reporting), which made its "drafting details, not fatal flaws" defense credible rather than evasive. Crucially, in the closing PRO turned CON's own framing against it: CON's proposed alternative (decoupling benefits from work entirely) is at least as unscheduled and undefined as anything PRO proposed, yet CON demanded PRO supply exact numbers while offering no comparable specificity for its own fix. CON never adequately answered this asymmetry, and its moat argument weakened once PRO recast the aggregator as public infrastructure rather than private cross-platform surveillance. CON's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost. On balance PRO ended the debate with the cleaner, more resolved comparison, while CON's most damaging point (the timing/aggregation contradiction) was answered well enough, even if not perfectly, to keep PRO's case standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Q2 pressure exchange: CON argued platforms would ration hours to dodge the threshold, but PRO's Q2 pointed out CON had also conceded no platform can see a worker's cross-platform total — forcing CON to soften "algorithmic gaming" into vague "probabilistic hedging," a visible retreat under direct pressure.</best_rebuttal>
